# Templates {.unnumbered}

A template is a maintained notebook for a complete procedure: selecting
observations, performing a calculation and saving interpretable results. Its
**parameters** cell specifies one run. Changing those settings lets you reuse
the procedure for another selection, model or experiment, or prepare many
independent jobs without maintaining a separate procedure for each one.

These fourteen templates cover behavioral analysis, fitting, simulation,
parameter exploration and pooled model comparison. Their defaults use the
**war-photo-recall experiment** as a shared worked example. The saved figures
and tables show that example; they are replaced when you execute a new run.
Choose a task below, then download its notebook and required inputs.

The procedures connect through saved products:

1. **Describe responses.** Analysis templates read observed or simulated response files,
   establish a pattern and expose discrepancies.
2. **Check a mechanism.** Parameter shifting starts from saved baseline parameters and
   examines controlled interventions without refitting.
3. **Fit configured models.** The single [fitting template](templates/fitting.ipynb)
   estimates parameters, saves fit records, optionally simulates, and compares configured benchmarks.
4. **Generate predictions.** [Simulation](templates/simulation.ipynb) produces saved
   responses from any configured collection of fits.
5. **Compare results.** [Model comparison](templates/model_comparison.ipynb) reads the
   saved fits and responses, relating likelihood, AIC, search variation and behavioral predictions.

The shared example compares ordinary CMR, source-only eCMR and broader eCMR. To inspect
completed runs, use the supplied fits and responses. To change the scientific specification,
configure the fitting or intervention procedure and pass its saved outputs to the analyses.
The [local instructions](#from-a-template-to-a-run) explain preparation and execution.

## The experiment

In this experiment, Dupertuys and colleagues asked whether emotion changes both
**which pictures people remember** and **the order in which they remember them**. Participants studied
photographs relating to the war in Ukraine, then recalled them from memory.
The final sample comprised 123 English-speaking adults selected for their
reported concern about the war.

Each participant completed four rounds, each with two phases:

1. **Study the photographs.** A list contained twelve target photographs, plus
   an extra “buffer” photograph at each end. Each image appeared for six seconds,
   followed by a three-second blank screen.
2. **Recall the photographs.** Immediately after the list, participants typed
   short descriptions of as many photographs as they could remember, in any
   order. They then continued to the next study-and-recall round.

Researchers later scored the typed responses by matching descriptions to
photograph identities, retaining the order in which the pictures were recalled.

The lists differed in their emotional composition. **Emotional** photographs
were rated as more negative and more arousing; **neutral** photographs were the
less negative, less arousing comparison images from the same war-related set.
Every participant encountered all three conditions:

| List condition | Target photographs in each list | Lists per participant |
|---|---|---:|
| Mixed | 6 emotional and 6 neutral | 2 |
| Pure emotional | 12 emotional | 1 |
| Pure neutral | 12 neutral | 1 |

List order was counterbalanced across participants, and target-picture order
was randomized within each list. Targets were not repeated across a
participant's four lists.

Mixed lists let us compare emotional and neutral recall within the same list.
Pure lists let us ask how that difference changes when the two types of picture
are studied separately. Recording recall order also lets us examine memory
search: for example, whether one recalled picture tends to be followed by a
picture studied nearby in time, or by a picture with similar meaning.

## The data used in the templates

The supplied file contains **492 list records**: 246 mixed, 123 pure-emotional
and 123 pure-neutral. Photographs are represented by item identifiers, and
recall responses by scored sequences. Buffer photographs are excluded, so the
study positions used in these templates refer to the twelve target photographs.
One pure-emotional record contains eleven valid target items and a padded slot;
the fixed-length analyses identify and exclude that record.

| Field | Meaning in these procedures |
|---|---|
| `subject` | Participant identifier, retained when simulating. |
| `list_type` | Whole-list condition: 1 = mixed, 2 = pure emotional, 3 = pure neutral. |
| `pres_itemnos` | Studied item codes within a trial; zero is a padded slot. |
| `pres_itemids` | Global picture identifiers used to align the distance matrix and categories. |
| `recalls` | One-based **study positions** of recalled items; zero is an unused response slot. |
| `valence` | Category at each study position: −1 = emotional, 0 = neutral. Check valid study items before counting categories. |

Study positions and item identities are different: a recall code of 3 points to
the third study slot, whose global picture identifier is found in `pres_itemids`.
The supplied distance matrix is indexed by global identifier minus one. Its
missing entries are outside the within-list comparisons used here; every
within-list pair required by the semantic examples has a finite distance.

Selections are made in notebook cells and leave the source file unchanged:

- **Fitting and pooled model comparison:** all 492 lists and all conditions.
- **SPC, PNR, stopping and temporal organization:** the 491 complete twelve-item
  lists. Each notebook explicitly reports the one excluded padded list.
- **Semantic organization:** the 246 mixed lists and the supplied distance matrix.
- **Category recall rate:** all conditions, with valid-item denominators.
- **Category SPC and category-CRP:** mixed lists by default.

Plots summarize each participant's selected lists before averaging across
participants. Error bars describe bootstrap intervals for those participant
summaries. Some bins have no variation or no defined values, so the current
plotters can report that a bootstrap interval is undefined; this does not turn
an unavailable category or transition into a zero-valued observation.

The observation file and distance matrix are the existing JAXCMR inputs, with no
extracts or recoding. The observation file also matches the ECMR3 project's copy.
All three fit records were prepared with the current library using the fitting
procedure below, including an independent recalculation of their objectives. [Fit provenance](templates/data/fits/README.md)
records their sources and assumptions. The response examples were produced by the simulation
template with ten repetitions per selected list and seed 1. Their JSON sidecars record the
parameters, selections and simulation settings. They are saved inputs to analysis; analysis
notebooks do not invoke fitting or simulation when an input is missing.

Each chapter has **Download notebook** and **Open in Colab** links beside its
contents list. Code starts collapsed; expand a labeled block to see the calculation,
or use the **Code** menu to show all code at once. Figures and tables remain visible.

## Run in Colab

Choose **Open in Colab** beside a chapter's contents list. Sign in to Google,
then choose **Runtime → Run all**. For the notebook opened from this repository,
Colab may ask you to confirm **Run anyway**. A standard CPU runtime is enough.

The setup cell installs JAXCMR from a pinned GitHub revision and downloads only
that notebook's supplied inputs, checking their hashes. This route works before
the PyPI release. Matching files are reused when setup runs again; a conflicting
file is preserved and reported. If you change a path to your own input, upload
that file through Colab's **Files** pane and keep the path consistent with the
parameters cell.

The SPC pilot completed on the default Python 3.13 CPU runtime without a restart.
If Colab requests one after installation, choose **Runtime → Restart session**,
then **Run all** again. The first raw cell contains Quarto page metadata; Colab
labels it “Unsupported Cell Type”, but skips it when running the code cells.

Results are written under the notebook's `output_dir` (for SPC,
`results/spc/spc.png`). In the **Files** pane, open that folder and use the file's
menu to **Download** the results. Download anything you want to keep before
Colab deletes the temporary runtime. Use **File → Download → Download .ipynb**
to retain an executed notebook, or **Copy to Drive** if you want a saved working
copy. The [VS Code setup](getting-started.qmd) remains the local route and still
awaits the planned PyPI release.

The Colab links use the `workshop-colab-2026-11-10` notebook revision. The setup cells install
JAXCMR and fetch the supplied inputs from commit `d919f1ad6aeacc7a36c40b96e365316219a7f40a`.
Analysis notebooks download the saved model responses; they do not run fitting or simulation.

## From a template to a run

Save downloaded notebooks in the working folder created during
[setup](getting-started.qmd), beside `data/`. Open the folder in VS Code, choose
its `.venv` kernel, edit the **parameters** cell and run the notebook from top
to bottom. Paths are relative to the working folder. Give independent runs
distinct output folders or run names so their results do not overwrite one another.

Settings are ordinary values: paths, numbers, lists, dictionaries and import
names. Imports, trial masks and model construction happen afterward, using the
effective values. The fitting template can select a model and its components,
objective, fitted parameters, participant subset and displayed analyses.
Analysis templates expose their trial selections and measure-specific settings. Their inputs are saved response files;
preparing or running an analysis does not generate missing simulations.

Ordinary imports occupy their own cell after the optional Colab bootstrap. Derived paths,
loading and calculations follow the injected parameters. `figure_str=""` displays figures
without saving them; a nonempty name saves under `figure_dir`. The defaults provide explicit
names for the worked examples. Subject-level CSV summaries use `output_dir`.

The analysis controls include repeated-item capacity (`size`), stopping `mode`, condition queries,
category fields and labels, and plot limits. Category recall also accepts configured paired
contrasts and contrasts of contrasts. Select these for the question being asked; the defaults
leave the optional tests empty.

You can also supply settings externally. [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/parameters.html)
and [Papermill](https://papermill.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage-parameterize.html)
use the same tagged cell. An override replaces a whole top-level value: to
change one model, supply the complete `model_configs` dictionary for that work unit.
Use `fit_alg_path` and `fit_hyperparams` to select and configure the optimizer. Analysis
templates use `data_paths` and `data_labels` for a collection; an explicit `data_path`
retains single-dataset use. Their condition queries are applied to each input.

### Execute a report with Quarto

With [Quarto installed](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/), you can execute a
notebook with overrides and render its results to HTML. For Python parameter
injection, Quarto also uses the Papermill package. Install it in the notebook
environment from the VS Code terminal:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pip install papermill
```

For example, run the PNR procedure for the third response and save a separate report:

```bash
QUARTO_PYTHON="$PWD/.venv/bin/python" quarto render pnr.ipynb --execute \
  -P query_recall_position:2 -P output_dir:results/pnr-third \
  --output pnr-third.html
```

Output positions are zero-based, so `2` means the third response. Use
`--execute-params settings.yml` for dictionaries or longer selections.
The explicit `--execute` runs the notebook; rendering an `.ipynb` without it
normally displays its stored results. The book itself displays stored examples.

### Prepare independent jobs with Papermill

For a cluster batch, it can be useful to inspect the complete set of jobs
before executing any of them. Papermill's `prepare_only=True` creates a
configured notebook for each job. The following Python cell prepares two
fitting runs that differ only in optimization seed and output folder:

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Prepare two fitting jobs without running them"

from pathlib import Path
from copy import deepcopy
import nbformat
import papermill as pm

source = nbformat.read("fitting.ipynb", as_version=4)
defaults = {}
parameter_cell = next(cell for cell in source.cells
                      if "parameters" in cell.metadata.get("tags", []))
# Evaluate only the parameter assignments, not the fitting procedure.
exec(parameter_cell.source, defaults)

jobs = Path("analyses/rendered")
jobs.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
for seed in [0, 1]:
    configs = deepcopy(defaults["model_configs"])
    for config in configs.values():
        config["seed"] = seed
    path = jobs / f"fitting_seed_{seed}.ipynb"
    prepared = pm.execute_notebook(
        "fitting.ipynb", str(path),
        parameters={"model_configs": configs, "output_dir": f"results/fitting-seed-{seed}"},
        prepare_only=True,
    )
    # Stored example results are not results from this new job.
    for cell in prepared.cells:
        if cell.cell_type == "code":
            cell.outputs = []
            cell.execution_count = None
    nbformat.write(prepared, path)
```

To prepare one model per job, pass a one-entry `model_configs` dictionary. Preserve the
project's chosen job boundaries: a model collection does not require running every model in
each scheduled job. Inspect the injected settings in each notebook. Execute one from the working
folder with:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m papermill \
  analyses/rendered/fitting_seed_0.ipynb analyses/rendered/fitting_seed_0.ipynb \
  --cwd .
```

The same prepared notebooks can be transferred with their inputs and run as
separate Slurm jobs, using the project folder as the working directory. This
matches the [remote-cluster workflow](https://github.com/githubpsyche/sbatch/blob/master/workshop/04-prepare-work-units.qmd):
maintain a procedure, prepare concrete work units, then schedule their execution.
Preparing jobs does not fit a model; rendering HTML is a separate presentation step.

For participant jobs, the fitting template uses `pooled=False` and
`subject_indices=[i]`, where `i` indexes the sorted participant IDs. Simulation
and parameter exploration can instead vary seeds or parameter values. Choose
the work unit around the scientific question and keep its inputs and outputs
explicit. A fit-only job sets both `redo_sims` and `redo_figures` to `False`;
later simulation can use its saved result.

## Modeling procedures

The example collection estimates nine continuous CMR parameters and ten for each eCMR
variant, using the same observations and termination-excluded likelihood. The two eCMR
specifications differ in whether emotional modulation also affects temporal association learning.
The default simulator conditions on observed recall counts. Recall length, stopping distributions
and pure-list category totals therefore are imposed; mixed-list category allocation and recall
organization can vary.

Simulation and parameter shifting start from the supplied fits without optimization. The latter
includes encoding-drift sweeps and a separate controlled temporal-emotional-modulation switch.
Model comparison consumes the saved fits and responses. Its results describe pooled solutions,
not independent participant estimates. Each procedure remains configurable for other inputs,
models and scientific questions.

| Procedure | Notebook | Required inputs |
|---|---|---|
| [Fitting models](templates/fitting.ipynb) | [Download](downloads/fitting.ipynb) | Observations; produces configured fits and optional responses. |
| [Simulating from saved fits](templates/simulation.ipynb) | [Download](downloads/simulation.ipynb) | Observations + named fit records. |
| [Exploring parameter effects](templates/parameter_shifting.ipynb) | [Download](downloads/parameter_shifting.ipynb) | Observations + baseline fit records. |
| [Comparing pooled model fits](templates/model_comparison.ipynb) | [Download](downloads/model_comparison.ipynb) | Observations + fit records + saved responses and provenance. |

## Adapting a procedure

Start by changing the settings cell: input paths, trial selection, parameters
and output folder. Check the meanings of item codes, participant identifiers,
categories and response padding before interpreting results. Retain the same
selection for comparisons that are intended to address the same observations.

The [remaining repository templates](https://github.com/githubpsyche/jaxcmr/tree/main/templates)
are research examples with varying dependencies and maintenance status. They
remain at their original paths and are outside this prepared set.
